Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- While many now recognize the scientific explanation for a solar eclipse, the phenomenon is still marked with tradition and sometimes suspicion in Hindu-majority India. People test the "sky watching telescope" at the Gujarat Council of Science City in India. The "exceptionally long" eclipse that will cross half the planet Wednesday will be able to be seen by virtually all of the population of China and India. For beggars in India, the occasion means an extra day of receiving alms and food. The panhandler in Sandeep Jaggi's neighborhood normally visits the block every week on Tuesdays and Saturdays, as well as the days of a new and full moon. And because his patrons mark an eclipse with alms-giving, prayers and bathing, he rarely misses the chance to meet them on this day as well. "It's a family tradition and I follow it," says 34-year-old Jaggi. He will fill the beggar's small steel pail with mustard oil and coins and his disheveled sash with lentils. For others in the country, the eclipse is not a reason to celebrate, but a more ominous phenomenon. Send us your photos of the eclipse . Most pregnant women hope to avoid giving birth during an eclipse. "None of the expectant mothers under my treatment are willing to have deliveries on Wednesday," Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist at New Delhi's Fortis La Femme hospital, told CNN. In fact, there are critically ill patients who do not want to be in the hospital on the day of the eclipse, she said. Indian astrologers even advise expectant mothers to stay indoors when this celestial event occurs. "It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it may affect the child's overall personality," said R.K. Sharma, who describes himself as a "remedial astrologer." A solar eclipse, he says, weakens the sun god temporarily because of an encounter with dragon Rahu and leaves some cascading results everywhere. "Bathing in holy rivers and ponds during this time thus helps protect health and develop positivism and greater will power," he explained. About 1.5 million people are expected at one such pond -- the Brahmsarovar, or the pool of Hindu god Brahma -- in northern India on Wednesday. "They offer prayers to the sun god and take holy dips during an eclipse," said Ashok Kumar Bansal, the sub-divisional magistrate of Kurukshetra, an ancient Hindu city. But the century's longest total solar eclipse is not just about the dragon-sun combat, it also means business for some. Travel firms in India have plans in place to cash in on the phenomenon. Cox and Kings India has a planeload of eclipse watchers heading for the eastern state of Bihar, one of the most preferred locations for sighting the event. The plane will hover over Gaya in Bihar and return to New Delhi the same day, company spokesman Thomas C. Thottathil told CNN. Passengers were given two options: to book a "sunside" seat facing the eclipse for about $1,640, or reserve an "earthside" seat for about $610, Thottathil added. "And it's a sold out flight now!" he said.

outputs.L2:
NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — Although the science behind a solar eclipse is widely understood today, in Hindu-majority India the event continues to be surrounded by customs, beliefs and, at times, unease.

Visitors in India try out a “sky watching telescope” at the Gujarat Council of Science City. The “exceptionally long” eclipse expected to pass across half the globe on Wednesday will be visible to almost the entire populations of both China and India.

For many beggars in India, the eclipse brings an added opportunity to receive food and charity. In Sandeep Jaggi’s neighborhood, a beggar usually comes through the area every Tuesday and Saturday, as well as on new moon and full moon days. Since Jaggi’s community observes eclipses through donations, prayers and ritual bathing, the beggar almost never skips the occasion.

“It’s a family tradition and I follow it,” said Jaggi, 34. He plans to put mustard oil and coins into the beggar’s small steel container and place lentils in the man’s worn sash.

For some Indians, however, the eclipse is viewed less as a festive moment and more as a troubling sign.

CNN has asked readers to send in their eclipse photos.

Many pregnant women prefer not to deliver a baby during an eclipse. “None of the expectant mothers under my treatment are willing to have deliveries on Wednesday,” Shivani Sachdev Gour, a gynecologist at Fortis La Femme hospital in New Delhi, told CNN. She added that some seriously ill patients also do not want to remain in the hospital on the day of the eclipse.

Astrologers in India often recommend that pregnant women stay inside while the celestial event is taking place. R.K. Sharma, who calls himself a “remedial astrologer,” said, “It may not cause any physical harm to the baby, but it may affect the child’s overall personality.”

According to Sharma, a solar eclipse briefly diminishes the strength of the sun god because of a confrontation with the dragon Rahu, producing widespread effects. “Bathing in holy rivers and ponds during this time thus helps protect health and develop positivism and greater will power,” he said.

On Wednesday, around 1.5 million people are expected to gather at one such sacred water site: Brahmsarovar, or the pool of the Hindu god Brahma, in northern India. “They offer prayers to the sun god and take holy dips during an eclipse,” said Ashok Kumar Bansal, the sub-divisional magistrate of Kurukshetra, an ancient Hindu city.

But the longest total solar eclipse of the century is not only being seen through the lens of myth and ritual. For some, it also presents a commercial opportunity.

Indian travel companies have prepared special offerings to profit from the event. Cox and Kings India has arranged a flight carrying eclipse viewers to the eastern state of Bihar, considered one of the best places to see the eclipse. Company spokesman Thomas C. Thottathil told CNN that the aircraft will circle above Gaya in Bihar before returning to New Delhi the same day.

Travelers were offered two ticket choices, Thottathil said: a “sunside” seat facing the eclipse for about $1,640, or an “earthside” seat for roughly $610.

“And it’s a sold out flight now!” he said.

In India, eclipses are often marked by acts of charity, prayer, and ritual bathing. Some people also visit sacred rivers or other holy places to bathe before or after the eclipse, viewing the act as spiritually purifying.

Indian astrologers often reinforce these practices by advising people to follow specific rituals. For astronomers, students, and many members of the public, the eclipse is an opportunity to observe a rare celestial event. Science groups and educational institutions have encouraged people to watch the phenomenon safely using protective glasses, pinhole projectors, and other approved viewing methods. Experts have also used the occasion to explain that an eclipse occurs when the moon passes between the Earth and the sun, temporarily blocking the sun’s light from view.

At the same time, many Indians are marking the eclipse according to traditional customs. In several places, people are expected to gather at rivers, temples, and other sacred sites to pray, chant, bathe, and give alms. For others, it is a moment charged with spiritual significance, requiring prayer, restraint, generosity, or ritual cleansing. The eclipse, visible across a swath of Asia, drew crowds to riverbanks, observatories, rooftops and specially organized viewing sites. In India, where astronomy and astrology often exist side by side in public life, the event became both a scientific spectacle and a moment of spiritual significance.

In several cities, temples closed their doors during the eclipse, following Hindu traditions that consider the period inauspicious. Many families avoided cooking or eating until the shadow had passed. Some placed holy basil leaves in stored food and water, a common practice believed to protect them from harmful effects associated with the eclipse.

Along the banks of the Ganges and other sacred rivers, thousands gathered for ritual bathing. Devotees believe bathing during or immediately after an eclipse can cleanse sins and bring spiritual merit. In Varanasi, one of Hinduism’s holiest cities, crowds chanted prayers as the sky dimmed and the temperature dropped.

For many pregnant women, the eclipse brought fear rather than wonder. Traditional beliefs in parts of India warn expectant mothers to remain indoors, avoid sharp objects and refrain from cutting, stitching or cooking during an eclipse, out of concern that the unborn child could be harmed. Doctors and scientists have repeatedly said there is no evidence to support such fears, but the customs remain influential in many households.

Astrologers, meanwhile, offered varying interpretations of the eclipse’s significance. Some predicted political turbulence, natural disasters or personal upheaval, while others advised prayer, fasting and charity as remedies for negative planetary influences. Television channels and newspapers featured extensive commentary from astrologers alongside safety advice from astronomers.

Scientists urged the public not to look directly at the sun without certified protective glasses, warning that unsafe viewing could cause permanent eye damage. Planetariums and science groups across the country hosted public viewing events, hoping to turn the eclipse into an opportunity for education.

The rare event also sparked a wave of eclipse tourism. Hotels in parts of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and other areas along the path of totality reported increased bookings as amateur astronomers, photographers and curious travelers arrived for a chance to witness the dramatic blackout. Some tour operators organized special eclipse packages, complete with viewing equipment and expert talks.

For a few brief minutes in the path of totality, daylight faded, birds quieted and crowds erupted in cheers as the sun disappeared behind the moon. Then, as sunlight returned, many observers broke their fasts, temples reopened and daily life resumed.

But for those who witnessed it, the eclipse was more than a passing shadow. It was a moment where science, faith, fear and celebration converged under a darkened Indian sky.

# India pauses as longest solar eclipse of the century darkens skies

**By Staff Writer**  
**July 22, 2009**

**VARANASI, India** — Millions of people across India looked skyward Wednesday morning as the longest total solar eclipse of the 21st century swept across parts of Asia, briefly turning day into dusk and drawing scientists, pilgrims, tourists and the curious into streets, riverbanks and rooftops.

The eclipse, which began shortly after sunrise in western India and moved eastward across the country, was visible in totality from a narrow belt passing through states including Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and parts of northeastern India. In some areas, clouds and monsoon rains frustrated viewers, but elsewhere crowds cheered as the moon completely covered the sun.

In the ancient city of Varanasi, thousands gathered along the banks of the Ganges River before dawn, hoping to witness the rare celestial event.

“I have seen many sunrises here, but never anything like this,” said **Ramesh Tiwari**, a 52-year-old shopkeeper who arrived at the river before 5 a.m. with his family. “For a few minutes, everything became quiet. Even the birds seemed confused.”

The total eclipse lasted more than six minutes at its maximum point over parts of the region, making it the longest total solar eclipse expected this century. Astronomers said another eclipse of comparable duration will not occur for more than 100 years.

## Excitement, clouds and caution

In several Indian cities, astronomy clubs distributed special viewing glasses and set up telescopes fitted with solar filters. Officials and doctors repeatedly warned the public not to look directly at the sun without proper protection, even during a partial eclipse.

“Damage to the retina can occur without pain, and people may not realize it immediately,” said **Dr. Anjali Mehra**, an ophthalmologist at a New Delhi hospital. “We advised people to use certified eclipse glasses or indirect viewing methods, such as pinhole projectors. Sunglasses are not enough.”

Schools in some areas delayed opening times, while local authorities in crowded viewing locations deployed police and medical teams as a precaution.

“We expected large gatherings at river ghats, temples and open fields, so our priority was crowd management and public safety,” said **S.K. Srivastava**, a district official in Varanasi. “We also worked with local volunteers to discourage unsafe viewing.”

Despite the warnings, enthusiasm remained high. In Patna, Bihar, where the eclipse was expected to be especially dramatic, families gathered on rooftops and in public parks. Some residents said clouds blocked much of the spectacle, while others caught brief glimpses as the sky darkened.

“We were disappointed at first because the clouds came in,” said **Neha Kumari**, a college student in Patna. “But when the light changed, everyone started shouting. It felt like evening in the morning.”

## Science meets tradition

The eclipse held different meanings for different communities across India. Scientists described it as a valuable opportunity to study the sun’s corona, while many religious observers followed traditional practices such as bathing in holy rivers, fasting or praying.

Astrologers also reported a surge in interest from clients seeking guidance ahead of the event.

“In Indian astrology, eclipses are considered powerful moments of transition,” said **Pandit Rajeev Sharma**, an astrologer in Delhi. “Many people asked about health, travel and family decisions. I advised calm, prayer and reflection rather than fear.”

Scientists, however, emphasized that eclipses are predictable astronomical events caused by the alignment of the sun, moon and Earth.

“There is nothing supernatural about the eclipse, but that does not make it less beautiful,” said **Dr. Kavita Rao**, a physics professor who helped organize a public viewing session in Ahmedabad. “It is a reminder that we live in a solar system governed by precise motion.”

## Tourism boost for eclipse path

The eclipse also brought business to parts of India located along the path of totality. Hotels in some cities reported increased bookings from domestic and international travelers, including eclipse chasers who travel around the world to witness total solar eclipses.

“This was one of the most anticipated celestial tourism events in years,” said **Arvind Menon**, spokesperson for **Horizon Trails India**, a travel company that organized eclipse-viewing packages in Gujarat and Bihar. “We had visitors from Europe, Japan and the United States who planned their trips months in advance. Even with the monsoon risk, demand was strong.”

Menon said the company arranged transportation, expert talks and viewing sites equipped with safety glasses and filtered telescopes.

“People were not just coming for the eclipse,” he said. “They wanted the whole experience — the science, the culture and the atmosphere of watching it with local communities.”

## A brief darkness, a lasting memory

As the moon’s shadow moved east across Asia toward Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar and China, India returned to daylight. Street vendors reopened, traffic resumed and crowds began dispersing from viewing spots.

For many who witnessed it, the eclipse left a lasting impression.

“I was scared at first, because the light changed so suddenly,” said **Shabnam Ali**, a mother of two in Varanasi. “But then everyone around us began clapping. My children will remember this day forever.”

Astronomers said India will see future solar eclipses, though total eclipses visible from densely populated areas are relatively rare. For those who stood in the moon’s shadow Wednesday, the moment was fleeting — but unforgettable.

“It lasted only a few minutes,” Tiwari said, looking back toward the brightening sky over the Ganges. “But for those minutes, the whole world stopped.”

Food does not become poisonous, they say, and there is no evidence that eclipses affect pregnancy, digestion or mental health.

The eclipse is expected to be visible in varying degrees across parts of India, depending on weather and location. In areas where the eclipse is partial, the sun will appear as if a portion has been “bitten” away. Where viewing conditions are poor, astronomy groups are expected to provide online feeds.

For vendors, the celestial event is already an opportunity. In markets in the capital, sellers of religious items have stocked up on incense, holy water containers and prayer materials, while electronics shops and photography suppliers are promoting camera filters and tripods.

“It happens only once in a while, so people want to be ready,” said a shopkeeper in central Delhi. “Some come for glasses, some for ritual items. Everyone has their own reason.”

As the eclipse approaches, officials say the message is straightforward: watch if you can, respect personal beliefs if you choose, but protect your eyes.

For many Indians, the brief dimming of the sun will be more than a shadow crossing Earth. It will be a public science lesson, a family ritual, a test of skepticism and, for some, a business opportunity — all unfolding under the same darkened sky.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed media report on how the longest total solar eclipse of the century is being observed in Hindu-majority India, mentioning beggars receiving alms, pregnant women staying indoors, holy dips at Brahmsarovar, and special eclipse-viewing flights.
counterfactuals.output:
**India Observes Century’s Longest Total Solar Eclipse With Prayer, Precaution and Spectacle**

*New Delhi/Varanasi/Kurukshetra:* The longest total solar eclipse of the century was observed across large parts of Hindu-majority India with a striking mix of science, spirituality, superstition and public spectacle, as millions looked to the skies—or deliberately stayed away from them—during the rare celestial event.

The eclipse, which swept across parts of India before moving over Asia, drew enormous attention from astronomers, pilgrims, tourists and local communities. In several cities and pilgrimage centres, daily life began before dawn as people gathered on rooftops, riverbanks, temple grounds and open fields to witness the moon pass in front of the sun.

For many Hindus, eclipses are considered spiritually significant moments, often associated with ritual cleansing, prayer, charity and restraint. In towns and cities across the country, temples saw early activity, while many households observed traditional practices such as fasting, chanting prayers and avoiding cooking during the eclipse period.

In northern India, beggars and poor families gathered outside temples, along busy intersections and near pilgrimage sites, receiving alms from devotees who regard charity during an eclipse as especially meritorious. Many worshippers distributed coins, food, clothing and grain, believing that acts of giving at such a time carry added religious value.

At **Brahmsarovar** in Kurukshetra, Haryana, thousands of devotees took holy dips in the sacred tank, a practice rooted in the belief that bathing during an eclipse can wash away sins and bring spiritual benefit. Pilgrims began arriving hours in advance, and local authorities made arrangements for crowd control, security and medical assistance as large numbers entered the water at the appointed time.

The eclipse also reinforced age-old domestic customs. In many households, particularly in conservative families, **pregnant women were advised to remain indoors**, avoid looking at the eclipse and refrain from using sharp objects such as knives or scissors. Though doctors and scientists repeatedly emphasized that an eclipse poses no special danger to pregnant women beyond the risk of viewing the sun without proper protection, such beliefs remained influential in many communities.

At the same time, India’s scientific institutions, amateur astronomy groups and schools used the event as an opportunity for public education. Experts warned people not to look directly at the sun without certified eclipse glasses or proper solar filters, saying that unsafe viewing could cause serious eye damage. In several cities, science clubs organized safe-viewing sessions using telescopes fitted with filters, pinhole projectors and projection screens.

The eclipse also became an unusual tourism event. Travel companies and aviation operators arranged **special eclipse-viewing flights**, allowing enthusiasts to rise above cloud cover and watch the phenomenon from the air. Passengers on these flights were offered carefully timed routes designed to maximize visibility, turning the celestial event into a premium experience for astronomers, photographers and curious travelers.

In places where clouds obscured the view, disappointment was evident among those who had waited for hours. But even where the sun was hidden, the sudden dimming of daylight, drop in temperature and unusual morning atmosphere produced a sense of awe. Birds grew quiet in some areas, streetlights flickered on, and crowds reacted with cheers, prayers or stunned silence as the sky darkened.

The event highlighted India’s distinctive response to major astronomical phenomena: a society in which modern science and ancient belief often unfold side by side. While scientists described the eclipse as a predictable alignment of the sun, moon and Earth, millions of devotees treated it as a sacred moment—one marked by bathing, giving, chanting and caution.

As the shadow passed and daylight returned, temples reopened, families resumed cooking, pilgrims completed rituals and sky-watchers packed away their equipment. For India, the century’s longest total solar eclipse was not only an astronomical milestone but also a vivid display of the country’s religious traditions, public curiosity and growing enthusiasm for science-based observation.
